title: Do video games produce real-life violence?
summary: Josh and Chuck examine whether violent video games produce real-life violence. They open with a 2006 German proposal (from Bavaria and Lower Saxony representatives) to jail people up to twelve months for virtual violence, prompted by the Sebastian Bosse school shooting, which wounded 37 people. They cover the difficulty of proving a causal link, the American Psychological Association's position, the book Grand Theft Childhood by Lawrence Kutner and Cheryl Olson and critic Guy Cumberbatch, the Devin Moore Alabama case, the Columbine lawsuit naming Sony, Nintendo, Time Warner and Palm Pictures, and the Indiana University brain-scan study. They present the case for a link (immersion, classical conditioning, script theory, TV studies) and the criticisms (anecdotal evidence, Lee Malvo's Halo claim, falling youth violence rates, ESRB rating problems, the small sample sizes). They conclude the issue is complex and the real question is which children are most at risk. The episode ends with a listener mail segment about gas chromatography mass spectrometry explained by Joe Christensen of Thomas More College, and a sign-off.

entities.name: Harvard Medical School Center for Mental Health and Media

segments.title: Opening banter and German violent game bill
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter, then Josh describes the 2006 German proposal by Bavarian and Lower Saxony representatives to jail people up to twelve months for virtual violence, following the Sebastian Bosse school shooting. They frame the core question of whether violent games cause real violence and say the evidence is unresolved.

segments.title: Why proving a link is hard
segments.summary: They discuss why it is hard to prove video games cause violence, noting the American Psychological Association's view that games are only one part of a larger problem. They quote Guy Cumberbatch from Grand Theft Childhood by Kutner and Olson criticizing how statistical tests are used in this research.

segments.title: Historical blame on media and the Devin Moore case
segments.summary: They note that violence has previously been blamed on TV, comic books and other media. They describe the 2006 Alabama case of Devin Moore, who played Grand Theft Auto, killed police officers and was sentenced to death. They mention the Columbine lawsuit against media companies, which cited The Basketball Diaries.

segments.title: Lawsuits, legislation and the prohibition analogy
segments.summary: They question where the line should be drawn for lawsuits over media that depicts violence, including films about Columbine. They compare banning violent games to alcohol prohibition and conclude that banning all violent media is unlikely.

segments.title: Arguments for a link: immersion, conditioning and brain scans
segments.summary: They outline the case that games cause violence: TV studies, immersion, and classical conditioning through reward systems. They discuss a 2006 Indiana University brain-scan study of kids playing Need for Speed Underground and Medal of Honor: Frontline, which found increased amygdala activity and decreased prefrontal cortex activity. They also mention the competitive-game and sports-rage cases.

segments.title: Hostility study, criticisms and script theory
segments.summary: They describe a meta-analysis-style study in which low-hostility kids who played violent games were more likely to fight than high-hostility kids who did not. They then cover criticisms: anecdotal evidence, Lee Malvo's Halo claim, falling juvenile violent crime, the small number of school shooters despite widespread play, and problems quantifying violence and ESRB ratings. They explain script theory.
topics: criticisms of video game violence research

segments.title: Conclusion: asking the right questions
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck discuss personal experiences with violent games, note that Columbine's shooters were already troubled, and conclude the issue is complex. The key question is which children are most at risk of being influenced, and the hosts say both sides have valid points.
topics: video game effects on the player

segments.title: Listener mail: gas chromatography mass spectrometry
segments.summary: A listener points out the abbreviation GC-MS. Joe Christensen, associate professor of physics at Thomas More College in Kentucky, gives a short explanation of how a gas chromatography mass spectrometer identifies molecular composition, and offers to help explain things in the future.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh asks listeners for explanations of prog rock and gives contact information for tweets, Facebook and email, then the episode ends.
